utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Strinovic, I would like now to go through the separate sections of binder 1 of the Exhibit 410 and answer specific questions. And first of all, in relation to tab 1, with your report and now also as tab 1 of this exhibit, you provided a chart giving the total number of 5.140 examined bodies and the forensic findings, and you also refer in this chart to the number of 11.834 killed that we saw in Mr. Grujic's report. Why is your number so much smaller?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can tell you is that there is the figure of 11.834 persons killed in Croatia. The figure of 5.140 refers to all those cases who were processed in the mortuaries in Zagreb, Osijek, Vinkovci, Rijeka and Virovitica. That is to say it is one number of cases which were investigated by forensic medical technicians and pathologists and a large number of cases did not reach the mortuary, so at the beginning of the war when there are a lot of victims, what was done was the causes of death were determined. They were mostly soldiers therefore, and the circumstances of their death and investigation was carried out on the field -- in the field without any autopsy examinations or any forensic professionals or pathologists taking part. So I think that that is why there is such a big difference. This was a war, it was a situation where we had a large number of dead, and quite simply, not all the bodies were taken to the mortuary or able to be taken to the mortuary, but a speeded-up process was applied, witnesses' testimony and the bodies buried.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now turning to tab 2. You have here the number of exhumed bodies given in total with 3.373. That's slightly smaller than the number that was given in Mr. Grujic's report. Can you explain why there is a difference?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can tell you is that this figure of 3.373 was obtained from the government office for missing persons and detainees, and that number changes almost daily. So if we had a date which corresponded to the figure, then we'd know. But all those -- all those figures came from the same sources, and the figure would change according to the date on which it was published.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what we have here under tab 2, that's the current situation in relation to exhumations and identifications?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I think that's what it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now, in your work did you also take part in exhumations and identification of victims of Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of our work, we did exhume and identify persons who were of Serb ethnicity from the very beginning of the war, so that already in 1991, the exhumation was conducted of part of the corpses of people who had fallen victim in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Strinovic, I do not want to go into details of these exhumations because it is outside of the Prosecution case, but in case the Judges or the parties would hear from you about such exhumations, you would be able to give details?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would. That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's now turn to tab 3, and you have here listed those findings in relation to paragraph 39 of the indictment, Vocin. What can you tell us about the Vocin crime scene in relation to your findings? Can you explain when you found the grave, what you did do with the bodies and so on.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to available data, it was the event that took place on the 13th of December, 1991 when 43 persons were killed in the vicinity of Vocin, and their bodies were discovered the next day and were dealt with at the morgue in Slatina near Vocin on the 17th of December, 1991. As you can see from this table here, there were 43 persons in all, 43 bodies, 30 of whom were shot dead, met their death through firearms, another from explosives and others from blunt objects and violent deaths such as knife wounds, burnings and so on. With six individuals, the cause of death was unknown. All I can tell you is that they were all civilians killed in their own homes or in front of their own thresholds. They were mostly elderly persons, men and women, and at the spot at which they were killed is where their bodies were found, which means the bodies weren't moved at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you see this -- got in contact with the bodies; immediately afterwards or --

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The employees of the Institute for Forensic Medicine carried out the autopsies on the 17th of December, 1991. That is to say we saw the bodies four days after the event, after they were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under tab 4, you have provided two photos, and what -- the photo in relation to the person Stojan Nenadovic, what does it tell us about the cause of death?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May we have the photograph displayed?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think that we need to have it on the ELMO, because we all have it in the binder, and I think it's not necessary to put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can explain it, how we see it. We have it in front of us. You can simply explain it. And if it is necessary to point something out, I think then it's only for the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you very much, yes. So this was one particular case. The person was a Serb. He was killed by being beaten with chains all over his body, and it was due to those beatings that there was a haemorrhagic shock that set in and ultimately death. It was an individual whose son was in the Croatian army, and we assume that's the reason he was killed. The other individual under number 23, this was a person who was killed by a blow from an axe, and we can see a very deep wound, typical for a wound being caused by a heavy sharp object like an axe. So this would be shown by the way he was hit on the head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't give the name on the photo. I can't see the name of this person. Do you know the name, whether it is someone from the schedule in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This particular individual was from Vocin, but I can't say any more than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, tab 5 is a surrogate. We always put a surrogate sheet in here when the underlying documentation is in the other binders. It would be mostly exhumation reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's now turn to tab 6. It's the chart related to the village Bacin and paragraph 40 of the indictment. What can you tell us about this scene?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an event that took place on the 21st of October, 1991, when we consider that these persons were killed and found on the 13th to the 23rd of March, 1997, in Bacin. And we found 58 bodies at that time. And as can be seen from the table, of those 58 individuals, 25 lost their lives through being shot by firearms, one individual suffered a trauma to the body, and three individuals once again were shot by firearms. One person, the cause of death there must have been an explosive device. With 28 of the bodies, we were not able to ascertain the cause of death. Let me also mention that Vocin is a gravesite which was very difficult to investigate, complex, because the bodies were very much impaired. We had to work on the ground, and those are the results that we obtained under those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have -- at tab 7, you have given one photo. Why did you select this photo?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This particular photograph was selected. It was one of the rare Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. ones where we were able to show the cause of death. So this is a photograph on which we can see a large part of the cranial bone and the defects that are typical for a shotgun wound. So this was death by shot from a firearm to the back of the head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under tab 8, you have given names of victims from the list in the indictment related to this count, and you have put abbreviations behind them. Can you explain what the abbreviations mean.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. For example, for the first individual, Jukic, "S" means a firearm wound, a bullet wound. With the second one, it was an explosive. The third and fourth individuals once again through bullet wounds. The following one, Kulisic, was a trauma by a blunt object. The last two individuals we don't list the cause of death; the cause of death was not known.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, just an explanation for the systematic of this binder. As far as we did not have exhumation reports in-house, Dr. Strinovic checked his documentation in Zagreb and made these findings so that we know the cause of death for these people. We had particularly asked him to give us the findings from his documentation. And you will find in the course of the binder, you will find these abbreviations again and again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's now turn to tab 9. That's Lipovanic, paragraph 42. What can you tell us about this scene?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I can tell you that it is the Lipovacka Dreznica near Rakovica which is the place, not Lipovanici. And the date is the 28th of October, 1991 when these individuals disappeared. The exhumation took place from the mass grave on the 12th of June, 1996, in Lipovacka Dreznica. The identification was conducted on the ground, in the field. And according to the indictment, there are eight names or, rather, seven individuals, actually, because one person's name is to be found twice, Bozincevic Franjo, in the indictment. So in fact, there were seven persons. Apart from that, in the indictment we see the surname of Cindric, Marija Cindric, and this person's name was actually Brozincevic Marija, and all these seven persons were identified. The cause of death established, which is indicated in the table where we can see that one individual lost their lives to being shot by a firearm, another through trauma caused by a blunt object, and the four other individuals probably again gunshot wounds. With one of the persons, the cause of death was unknown.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, Dr. Strinovic just pointed out that Franjo and Franje is the same person. So there's only one Franjo who was in the grave and was killed. And the name for Marija, the surname for Marija is a different one than given here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to tab 11, Vukovici, what can you tell us about this?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an event that took place on the 7th of November, 1991, when these persons disappeared. And they were exhumed on the 13th of August, 1996. In the Vukovici hamlet, we found two persons on the indictment who were identified. They are Vukovic Nikola and Vukovic Ivan, and they were killed from a firearm. They were shot. Of the others on the indictment, let me say that there are data according to which these individuals were all killed through burning. They were all burnt. I should like to mention in this regard that there is some difference in the surnames. In the indictment we have Matinovic as one surname, Matinovic Joso and Matinovic Nikola. Those were the other names. However, it was Matovina Josip and Matovina Nikola. Matovina was the surname. In the Vukovici hamlet we found a site where the burning had taken place with at least four bodies, but we can assume that in fact the seven people listed in the indictment lost their lives at that same spot. Let me also add that in Vukovici, we found the bodies of two other persons, and we have ascertained the cause of death. They are Loncar Ivan and Loncar Milan, bothers, and they were found hanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you found -- you could actually identify four bodies burned, but how can it be that there are still more burned? How did you make the finding that it should be more than four? You give here at least six burned, in your schedule. How could you determine that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In the list it says that there were a total of at least six bodies. Of that number, at least four were burnt, and as to two persons, those two were hanged. So the remains of bones were found, and those bone remains indicated that there were at least four persons, four bodies. Now, whether there were more bodies, we cannot say for sure because, due to the high temperatures, the bones were very much damaged when they were burnt. Some of them might have been completely destroyed, leaving no traces at all. So once again, let me say there was a total of six individuals, two of whom were hanged, and at least four -- so we have proof to show that four persons had been burnt, their remains found. As to the rest, we didn't find any remains, which does not exclude the possibility that they were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now we turn to tab 14. Yes, tab 14, Saborsko, paragraph 44 in the indictment. What were your findings there?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 12th of November, 1991, persons went missing in the Saborsko area, and they were found and exhumed on the 13th of October, 1995, when we discovered 27 bodies, which can be seen from the table attached. We were also able to ascertain the cause of death. With one person it was a wound from a firearm, traumas in six individuals, and six others other causes, burnings, and so on; we found the remains of bones. With 15 bodies, the cause of death was not ascertained. We were not able to establish the cause of death for 15 persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And under tab 15, you have given again names that you checked in your office.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. So we have the names of four persons from the indictment where we can see the causes of death, such as trauma, other causes, gunshot wounds, and once again another cause of death. And four additional names which are not in the indictment but which were found in the Saborsko area. They were four persons who had been burnt to death.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you identify the burned victims?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without the protocol and records, it's difficult for me to say how we did this, but what I can tell you is the following: In cases where we had extensive burns in the sense of seeing that the bodies had been burned, shut up in wooden houses which were burnt to the ground, what we found there were just the remnants of bones, very small bone fragments. And then with the analysis conducted by an anthropologist, we ascertained whether they were human bone fragments and how many bodies were found on the spot. Then we obtained information from family members and witnesses who told us how many people had been shut up in those houses and what their names were. So in this way, combining the two, we were able to solve most of the cases on the basis of witness testimonies and on the basis of the number of bodies we found in the houses, and we were able to disclose the fate of those persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have actually, under tab 16, provided one photo, and it's the victim Kata Matovina. How could you be sure that it's her? How did you ascertain that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this photograph, we can see the types of remains that are left of a human body after they have been burnt in a house, when a fire has been going on for days and when all the bodily parts have been burnt, the house as well and the bodily tissue, except for some small bone fragments. This person was in a bed, she was immobile, and we know which part of the house she was to be found in. When we conducted the exhumation and investigated the burning site, in one part, in the room of Kata Matovina herself, we found some small bone fragments which, according to the anthropologist, corresponded to just one person, one body. Apart from that, we also found small fragments of teeth and bones which confirmed that it was elderly female and to all intents and purposes, judging by these findings, it would indicate that it was in fact this woman Kata Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Matovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's turn now to tab 17. That's Skabrnja 1, paragraph 45 of the indictment. You have here complete figures of the cause of death. What -- what enabled you to be so precise here in relation to each and every body?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Skabrnja 1, these were persons who were killed between the 18th and the 19th of November, 1991, and they were handed over through the Croatian side on the 23rd of November, 1991, which means four days after the event. So these were persons in a good -- in good condition, so they were easily identifiable. And the protocols that we have here of the post-mortems are quite clear, and the cause of death was clearly ascertained, as can be seen from this table.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now I would like to turn to tab 19, and it is the -- the scene Nadin. That's number 46 -- paragraph 46 in the indictment. What can you tell us about this?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As in the case of Skabrnja 1, in the case of Nadin 2, this was an event that took place on the 26th -- no. I'm sorry. On the 19th of November, 1991, when the persons were killed. And on the 26th of November, they were handed over to the Croatian side and a post-mortem was carried out that same day. The bodies were well preserved, all seven persons were identified, and the cause of deaths ascertained; these were gunshot wounds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now let's turn to tab 21. That's Skabrnja 2, paragraph 47 in the indictment. Can you explain your findings here.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Skabrnja 2 refers to an event of the 18th of November, 1991, up until February 1992. The persons were killed, and they were exhumed on the 6th of June, 1996, when it was established that there were 21 persons for whom we established the cause of death. For 14, gunshot wounds; 4, explosions; and 3 traumas with a blunt object provoking death.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have also under tab 22 created a list where you actually have given the cause of death in abbreviation behind each person. Yes?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was -- did -- did you get any information with the -- one of these persons was detained in the Knin prison?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Skabrnja 2, I have no such information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Then we turn now to tab 23. That's Bruska. What can you tell us about Bruska?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are persons who were killed on the 21st of December, 1991. They were exhumed on the 26th of April, 1996, when nine persons were identified. And for six, the cause of death was established. Actually, they first went missing and then they were found. One person who was also exhumed on that day at the gravesite in Bruska or, rather, Rodaljice, they were exhumed at the cemetery at Rodaljice. There is also a person called Josip Marinovic who died on the 10th of June, 1992, as a result of mistreatment in Knin prison. This information was obtained from the District Court in Zadar who ordered that these bodies be exhumed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have provided actually the -- under tab 24, the information from the court that you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness provided this document only during the preparation for his testimony. We have not yet a translation. We would provide it later when it is done. That's tab 24.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's now turn to tab 26. That's Ovcara, and paragraph 49 in the indictment. Can you explain how you heard about this crime scene and what your observations then were?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When talking about Ovcara, the beginning date is the 19th to the 20th of November, 1991, when the disappearance was reported of 255 persons from the hospital in Vukovar, and all trace of them was lost at the time. An investigation was started in the sense of searching for a grave where the victims taken from the hospital in Vukovar may be, and the first trace of a gravesite was discovered in 1992 when Dr. Clyde Snow discovered remains of human bones close to the Ovcara farm, and that is why we refer to it as the Ovcara case. In 1993, the first exhumation was started as a trial, which was soon stopped after it was begun. After that, the area was guarded right up until 1996 when, in September, the exhumation of bodily remains started fully, exhumation as well as the processing of bodies done by international experts. The exhumation lasted for a month and a half, upon which the bodies were taken to the forensic institute in Zagreb where data were further processed, and the bodies were handed over to the Croatian side only at the beginning of 1997. From the moment of exhumation until the completion of the processing of the bodies, experts from Croatia as well as local Serbs or experts from Serbia were present throughout, so that these were experts from both sides who were present both at the site of the exhumation and later on when the processing was done in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Strinovic, you mentioned a Dr. Clyde Snow, who was -- what kind of a person was he? Did he belong to any organisation?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was invited by the United Nations. Now, exactly which organisation he belonged to, I don't know, but he was invited by international organisations to take part in the search and exhumation of the remains of the persons who were killed at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that in 1993 exhumations started but stopped. Why did they stop? Why was it not done?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the Serb side insisted that the exhumation be stopped. Now, the reason behind this is something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "the Serb side," whom do you mean? If you don't know, just say you don't know.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you explain -- can you explain now tab 27, how we should read this table. The case is that -- we have here the column "Case." Are these the individual bodies or what does it mean, this number?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I should like to complete my comments on the previous table. I thought that this was just an introduction. I don't think we've completed addressing the previous table. So may I add a few brief remarks and then answer this question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this table, which is to be found on page 27, we see the causes of death for 188 persons who were killed with firearms, six with a blunt object, which means trauma. In one case, it was probably a gunshot wound, and in four cases it was not possible to ascertain the cause of death. So these were the 200 bodies found in the grave near Ovcara. Also, may I add very briefly that among the 200 bodies, 86 it was ascertained that they were wounded persons. As for the others, it was not possible to establish whether they had any wounds as they had been taken from the hospital. The average age of the persons found at Ovcara was 32 and a half, so the range was between 16 and 72 years of age. Among them there were two women. Those would be my comments. As for this table that you asked me about showing first the case or, rather, the number of cases, from 1 to 200, how the bodies were taken out of the gravesite, put in body bags and marked with numbers 1 to 200. The date is the date when the exhumation was carried out. Then the anthropologist, the name of the person who carried out the exhumation and later identification. The sex of the person; then the age, the range, minimum-maximum, the probable age; then the height, the range of the height, minimum-maximum; and the pathologist who carried out the post mortem. Then came the column "Cause of death" to indicate that they were killings, murders in all cases. And the last column, the probable identification. So these were persons who, after processing, provided sufficient elements to be able to be identified with a high degree of probability. This was 1996/1997 when for 57 persons it was possible to assume who they were. That is the last column regarding identity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the next, tab 28. That's a table where you can connect the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. body number with the name of the victim after identification; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. One can see exactly the number of cases, 1 to 200, the first and last names of the identified persons. And as I have already said, 190 persons have been identified to this day, ten still remain unidentified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the identification process still ongoing?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The process of identification, though it started in 1997, continues. It started by applying classical methods, findings obtained from anthropologists and forensic experts, and on the basis of their findings, it was possible to identify some 100 persons. After that, over the last three years, we are relying on DNA analysis for the identification of the remaining cases which it is not possible to identify applying classical methods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have provided under tab -- or, rather -- no. It's from the Prosecution documentation on Ovcara. You have here selected, under tab 29, some photos, and can you please briefly just explain what we see on the photos. The first photo, is that --

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first photograph shows the location where the gravesite is, the Ovcara gravesite. You can see a blind -- a mild hollow which caused people to suspect that there may be a grave there. Though there is vegetation and trees around it, this was where trial digging was done, and already on the surface, some bones were found which was a clue of the existence of a mass grave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the second photo?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the second photograph, we see the stage when parts of bodies are shown. So the exhumation was done so that first all the bodies were taken out and then one by one. So we can see the surface layer where it is possible to see dozens of bodies protruding from the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next photos, do they refer to a particular victim? It's called here number 5.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each of these victims with a number already has a name, first and last. Five photographs show only how these victims were thrown one on top of another and mixed together, so how difficult it was to take out each of those bodies without mixing up the remains of different persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And you have here a photo with the number 112 and two more photos related to this person. Who is he or was he?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a Croatian journalist, Sinisa Glavasevic, a person who reported about the events in Vukovar from August 1991 until he was captured and killed. So he was a reporter. This shows the spot where he was found and the number under which he was registered. Then on the second photograph you see the white bag in which his body was placed, as was -- were the bodies of all other persons, and taken to the Zagreb mortuary. And then you see the dentures of the person, and it is easy to see, even a layman can see that certain treatment was given to the teeth. And as each of us have -- has a different situation regarding his teeth, so that the reporter could be recognised on that basis too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the next two photos relate to the body number 1. You picked these photos. What can you tell us about these photos?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These photographs marked the number 1, it was the first body that was exhumed at Ovcara, showing two injuries, one on the right side of the head, a gunshot wound, an entry wound, and on the left-hand side, at the temple, an exit gunshot wound, so it was a shot that went through the skull.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Let's now turn to tab 31. That's Baranja 1, paragraph 50 in the indictment. What can you tell us about this gravesite and this case?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an event that took place on the 21st of September, 1991, when the persons went missing, and they were found on the 23rd of February, 1998 in a mass grave in Celija. We have here 11 persons from the indictment. In the case of six, we have the causes of death, as can be seen from this table. In the case of 15 persons, the cause was trauma, that is blunt object, in the opinion of the pathologist. There were damages on the bones that led them to conclude that they were caused by a blunt object, and that is why that was indicated as the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And under tab 32, you have given us these six persons that you particularly checked in your institute. Is that what it means?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The names of six persons for whom the cause of death is visible. As has already been stated, all of them were killed with blows from a blunt object.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now turning to tab 33. That's Baranja, cases 2 and 3, paragraph 51 in the indictment. What were your findings there?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an event of the 4th of October, 1991, when the persons went missing, and they were found in several stages. In September 1999, in Ilok, they were transferred from the SFRY in November and December 2002. A total of 17 persons of whom 13 died through gunshot wounds, one due to trauma, two probably through gunshot wounds, and for two, the cause of death was unknown. One of these persons, Vinko Oroz was captured in Baranja, then he was in Borovo Selo and Dalj, and he was delivered on the 11th of November, 1998, from Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the person Marinko Somodjvorac, was he also transferred from Novi Sad?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to this group of people, you have under tab 35 provided some photos. What can you tell us in relation to the photos? Why did you select these photos?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the case of Vinko Oroz, a person who was captured and then found in Novi Sad, this was a person clearly killed by firearms. You can see a gunshot wound with the entry wound, taken from the inside of the skull. It is a typical wound and was quite certainly caused by firearms. Also, Somodjvarac Marin there's also a clear gunshot wound found at the back of the head and it is an entry wound, so clearly the person was killed by a gunshot wound to the back of the head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Dr. Strinovic, apart from the cause of death of these people, how did you know how these people were captured and delivered somewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The information was obtained from the government Commission for Detained and Missing Persons who found this out, and I have conveyed it to you. So I don't know. I obtained the information from the government commission regarding the movement of these persons from the moment they went missing until they were discovered in Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like now to turn to tab 36, Lovas minefield, paragraph 52 in the indictment. What were your findings there?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an event of the 15th of October, 1991, when the persons were killed, and they were discovered in a mass grave in Lovas on -- between the 2nd and 9th of June, 1997. There were 21 persons from the indictment. All of them were identified. And the cause of death in eight cases were gunshot wounds; in one, a combination of gunshot and explosive device; in one, trauma. For six cases, probably the cause of death was gunshot wounds. An explosive device was the cause -- probable cause in one case, and for four persons it was not possible to ascertain the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And you have also provided here one photo, under tab 37, from one of the victims. And what kind of a cause -- what cause of death could you conclude from what you found in relation to this person?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is a person from the indictment, an injury to the head, a roundish, irregular defect on the skull which was probably caused by a gunshot wound. So that was the cause of death, probable cause of death.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We turn now to tab 38. That's Erdut 1, paragraph 53 in the indictment. What were your findings in relation to these bodies? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an event of the 9th of October, 1991, in Erdut. The persons went missing on that day, and they were exhumed on the 14th of October, 1998, in a mass grave at Celija. These were -- 11 persons were involved. The causes of death for four persons were gunshot wounds; for three, trauma; for three, probable gunshot wounds; and in one case the cause of death is unknown.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have provided, tab 39, the cause of death for two people where the Prosecution didn't have any documentation in-house. And you also provided, under tab 40, two photos. Can you explain the photos?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are persons -- that is correct. After that, two photographs are shown of two persons figuring in the indictment. In both cases, they are gunshot wounds. You can see a regular injury to the head which indicates with certainty that these were gunshot wounds to the head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now tab 41. That's Erdut case 2. Can you tell us about your findings.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an event that took place on the 9th of October, 1991. Three persons went missing and were later found in a mass grave in a well in Borovo Selo. They were exhumed on the 20th of September, 2000. So three persons were found and identified, and in the case of all three, the cause of death was gunshot wounds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in relation to tab 42, there is another Erdut case with one person. It's case 7, paragraph 53. What can you tell us about this body?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an event of the 3rd of June, 1992, when the person went missing and was found in a well in Dalj Planina, Dalj mountain, on the 26th of September, 2000, a person who was identified, and the cause of death is unknown.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's now turn to tab 43, Erdut Klisa, paragraph 54 of the indictment. Please tell us your findings there.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an event that took place on the 11th or, rather, November 1991. Five persons who went missing and were found in the mass grave in Celija and were exhumed on the 14th of October, 1998. All five individuals have been identified. The causes of death can be seen from the tables. Four were the result of gunshot wounds, and one cause of death remained unknown.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have also given us two photos in relation to -- in relation to two of the victims. And what can we see from the photos?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the photographs, we see the gunshot wounds in the head, irregular wounds. And on the second photograph, we can see at least three gunshot wounds to the head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning to tab 45, Vukovar, paragraph 54 and 55. What can you tell us here?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an event that took place on the 20th of November, 1991. That's the date when these persons disappeared. And they were found in two localities, one in Dalj at the Catholic cemetery there on the 3rd of March, 1998, which was when 11 victims were found. And in Dalj proper, or the Lovas farm, 24 victims were found there on the 17th of April, 2001. As we can see from the tables shown here, for the gravesite in Dalj, there were -- there was one case, probably of a gunshot wound, nine probably killed by explosives, and one individual whose cause of death remains unknown. In the Lovas farm gravesite, there were 20 gunshot wounds, one probably gunshot wound, two traumas, and one cause of death remains unknown.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have also provided under tab 46 the cause of death for several of the victims. That is what you checked in your files in Zagreb; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm now turning to tab 47, paragraph 56 in the indictment, Erdut case 4. Can you explain your findings here.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date of this event is the 10th of December, 1991, when these persons went missing. They were found in the well in the district of Dalj on the 28th of October, 1998. Three persons were found and identified, and the causes of death as established were as follows: With two individuals, it was trauma; with one person, it was probably a gunshot wound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have also provided, under tab 48, two photos. What can we see from the photos in relation to actually two persons?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These photographs refer to two persons. With the first person, we can see the fragments, bone fragments, of the head, the lower jaw, in fact, and the upper jaw and face. So on the basis of findings of this kind, the person conducting the autopsy noted that trauma was the cause of death, caused by a blunt object to the head which resulted in bone fracture. The second photograph shows part of the bones of the skull, which was fragmented. And let me say that very often the bones of the head suffer several fractures and are in pieces, the bones are fragmented, so it is difficult to reconstruct them. But here we can see on that part of the skull a regular defect on the lower part of the bone and a round defect which indicates that a gunshot wound was the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning now to tab 49, paragraph 57 in the indictment, Erdut case 5. Can you explain your findings.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an event that took place on the 26th of December, 1991, when these persons went missing. Their bodies were discovered in the Daljski Atar well on the 28th of October, 1998. There were seven persons on the indictment. We found six persons who were identified, and the causes of death in five cases were gunshot wounds, in one case probably gunshot wound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have provided several photos under tab 51. Can you explain the photos.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the photographs, you can see the causes of death. On the first photograph, you see the bone of the skull with the round defect, which indicates a gunshot wound. The second photograph shows the body which is fairly well preserved, and you can see the direction of the channel which shows the metal rod moving from the neck to the roof of the skull where there's a large defect, an entry wound to the head and neck from a firearm. On the following picture, we can once again see this same kind of gunshot wound. As I say, the body is well preserved. You can see the soft tissues. And on the skull there is a large irregular defect, and the rod which indicates the direction of the channel. And what you can see on the skull is the exit wound to the skull. On the following picture, this same case showing it when the bone has been cleared up, and you can see the exact trajectory. What is at the back is the exit wound. What you -- or entry one. What you see on the front is the exit wound. So the person was shot in the back -- from the back. And the last photograph shows once again a wound to the skull at the nape of the neck, and it is a round defect of the gunshot-wound type.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mrs. Uertz-Retzlaff, if we could go back to -- briefly to tab 45.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You can note paragraph 54, and you said it refers to Vukovar. According to the indictment, it says Klisa, Erdut case 3. It says here Catholic cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I understand that the Catholic cemetery is the place where the bodies were found.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Erdut case 3 and Vukovar are the same thing. That's my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. The grave -- the Catholic cemetery Vukovar is the grave, I believe. So that's why I mentioned Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But the witness said Dalj, Catholic cemetery at Dalj.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Strinovic, just to confirm, we have listed here paragraph 54 Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of the indictment related to an incident in Klisa also concerning the Erdut training centre, and you have here mentioned Catholic cemetery as the grave. Which Catholic cemetery?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we talking about paragraph 54, Erdut Klisa? Is that what we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the moment we're talking about tab 45 in the binder, and your tables refer to paragraph 54 in the indictment and 55 in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph? Paragraph 45 is Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. It was tab -- tab 45 in the binder. Tab 45 in the binder, not paragraph 45 in the indictment. If you look at your tables. And it refers in your table to paragraph 54 in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just make something clear? It seems that there is a printing error linked to paragraph 54. It is paragraph 55, both for the Catholic cemetery and the Dalj Lovas paragraph. It is the same table. So it must be paragraph 55, the Catholic cemetery, and paragraph 55, Dalj Lovas farm. In the Croatian text that I handed over to you it says paragraph 55 for both.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have actually detected a mistake in the table done in the translation. I'm sorry for this.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But if you compare the names given by Dr. Strinovic on the -- in tab 46, they correspond with the Annex 55. Yes. Thank you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe that we were talking now about tab 52. That is paragraph 58 in the indictment, Erdut 6. What were your findings in relation to this?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This event took place on the 21st of February, 1992, when four persons went missing who were subsequently found in the mass grave of the Daljski Atar on the 28th of October, 1998. They were four individuals. For one, a gunshot wound was the cause of death; for another it was gunshot plus explosive; and with one a trauma in one case, probably once again caused by an explosion. So those are the four persons identified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you did provide also under tab 53 several photos. Can you explain the photos.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the first photograph you can see once again part of the skull bone with a regular defect; once again a gunshot wound with this first individual. On the second photograph we see the bones of the head with a large defect that can be seen in the area of the eyes and forehead. A large portion of the bone is missing, and the person conducting the autopsy considered that the injury was caused by a blunt object which destroyed this part of the skull. On the following photograph, Helena Albert was the person. A combination of gunshot and explosive wounds. We can see the skin underneath the hair and the nape of the neck where there is a large irregular defect which could have been caused by either a gunshot wound or injuries caused by explosives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And now turning to tab 54, Grabovac, paragraph 59 in the indictment. And your findings, please.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This took place on the 4th of May, 1992, when five persons went missing. They are contained in the indictment, and their bodies were found in Beli Manastir on the 15th of April, 1998. Otherwise, they were transferred from another grave and location in Tikves. The cause of death, one gunshot wound, two probably caused by explosives, and with two persons the cause of death was not established.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Attached -- this should conclude the binder, and I have actually only one more question, and that relates to Dubrovnik. You have not provided any documentation in relation to Dubrovnik and the casualties there. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through the government department, I tried to get information about the victims in Dubrovnik, but I did not receive them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your office was not dealing with the bodies of the Dubrovnik schedule in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, that concludes my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Strinovic, just one question before I actually go ahead with the individual cases. You mentioned in your testimony a large number of locations, sites, which relate to persons who lost their lives, were killed during the war, et cetera. As far as I heard throughout the examination-in-chief, the only place which you mentioned and which is located in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or Republic of Serbia is Novi Sad; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So all the other places that you mentioned are outside the territory of Serbia or, rather, outside the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Is that right, Dr. Strinovic?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this Novi Sad that you mentioned reminds me of something that Judge Kwon asked you about, whether you knew who was where when. Now, do you know that in Novi Sad at the cemetery there, the bodies found in the Danube were exclusively buried there, bodies flowing down the Danube and floating down the Danube. Do you know how those bodies came to be in Novi Sad and buried there?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, these bodies that are exhumed in the Novi Sad cemetery got to Novi Sad in the river Danube. They were found on the banks of the Danube River, and after that, taken to Novi Sad where the autopsies were conducted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not only on the banks; they were floating along the river. And when the citizens or the authorities see a body floating down the river, then the police is called in, the border police, and they collect up those bodies, or that body, and these persons were taken out of the waters of the Danube and buried in Novi Sad. So there is no indication at all that any of these victims fell victim on the territory of the Republic of Serbia at all. Do you have any indications that any of these casualties were actually killed on the territory of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can do is repeat what I've already said. What I know about this is that the bodies were found at the cemetery in Novi Sad. They were exhumed there, and it is assumed that they were Croatian citizens and then their bodies were transferred to Zagreb where the bodies were identified, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Strinovic. When were these bodies handed over to you?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said on several occasions, this was already in 1991 -- no. 1999, I'm sorry, and then 2001, 2002, and they're still coming in. Those bodies are still coming in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. So already in 1999, the authorities, the Yugoslav authorities, that is, handed over to you the bodies for which they -- which were buried as persons unknown at the cemetery on Novi Sad because they were floating down the Danube and for whom it could have been assumed that they were victims from the conflicts that took place in Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, and so on. And that was within the frameworks of cooperation that you said was ongoing from 1991. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. As we've cleared up that matter and as it is the only place found on the territory of Serbia, Novi Sad, and as it is not a location where somebody lost their lives but only a place from which you received the bodies, you therefore have no information that anybody could have been killed on the territory of Serbia; right? Of the ones you studied, the cases you studied and mentioned.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have no information of that kind. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now I'd like to proceed and move on to your testimony. You say in your statement, under point 4, that as a member of the government commission, and I'm quoting you, I'm sure you'll recall this, nothing malicious there. "As a member of the government commission, I was coordinator for the medical team in the process of exhumation and identification. That was the agreement that was made, that there should be a physician, a specialist in forensic medicine present at each of these exhumation cases. During the exhumations that took place in 1995, I attended these on many occasions although the other physicians doing this work supervised most of the exhumations." Have I quoted you correctly? The paragraph starts, "As a member of the government commission..."

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think you have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And what emerges from this quotation, in fact, does it emerge that you, Professor Strinovic, did not have any personal, if I can put that way, personal, professional insight in the work of the teams for the exhumations which you supervised?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about the criteria applied to your profession, on that basis.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already stated, the teams were selected from all over Croatia, and they covered the whole of Croatia, and I was the person, just the person who determined the groups to go to which localities, which gravesites to conduct the exhumations, and then the processing and investigation and the transport of the bodies for further investigation. But they were individual teams made up of experts who actually did this work. So I didn't supervise their work specifically at each site.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what I understood you to say. So it was on behalf of the government that you did all this work. You organised the work, you sent the individual teams and individuals to the different localities, so you were the man in charge of all this on behalf of the government; right? I'm talking to the professional part of the work.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. That is connected to the professional part, the medical part, exhumation, identification, processing, that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Now, tell me, does that mean, and I'm not quite clear on this point, that each and every report on an exhumation would have to be verified and certified by you? Does that mean that or not?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Every report on exhumation was submitted to the government department headed by Mr. Grujic, who was present with the majority -- when the majority of these exhumations took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But he's not an expert in that field. But when I say verified by you, I meant professional verification, in your professional capacity. So it was not your duty to verify all the reports. That didn't come under your duties, did it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So all these jobs that you're testifying about were supervised by other physicians, actually, and as far as I understand you, you would just from time to time visit the sites, visit some of the locations. Would that be the standard practice that you applied? Would that be what your activities entailed?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, at the very beginning of our exhumations, I was present, and I conducted some of them myself. From the medical aspect, I was in charge of them. Later on, my colleagues took over this role, and so my colleagues would go to perform the exhumations at the different sites.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Strinovic, let's just understand each other here. I'm not challenging your professional qualities at all. Quite the contrary, I am saying that in view of your -- the direct work you did, and as far as I understood, you would from time to time tour the localities. So I'm not talking about the competent supervisor. I don't mean in the sense of your professional qualities, I mean in the sense of the work you did when you toured these localities. You were not there as a supervisor to control the professional work of those teams. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That is right, because usually there would be one doctor with one assistant, and they were in charge of one site, one locality, and covered the site from start to finish.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. So your opinion could not be - how shall I put this? - accepted as some -- as competent supervisor to be accepted by one and all, who would control that there and supervise it all, because you didn't actually do the work yourself; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In most of the cases, that is right. I was not there myself. My other colleagues conducted the work and were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. That's why I said that I wasn't -- it wasn't a competent supervisor whose opinion could be absolutely or relatively accepted as right, not in view of your professional qualities, of course, but in view of the activities you did and were linked to this. So we've cleared that up. Now, in paragraph 10, you say that in the process of your work, forensic medical professionals were used and only in other cases were pathologists used. That's what you say. Now, can we agree that the work of a pathologist engaged in exhumations is completely unacceptable or, rather, can we say that it is incompetent?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What does that mean? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I have understood that this is not clear to Mrs. Retzlaff either or to you, I see. That is why I wanted Professor Strinovic to explain it to you, to explain the difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let him have the report, first of all, which the accused is quoting from. Let him have a copy of his report.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is the problem, Mr. May? I am asking Professor Strinovic whether he can agree with me that the work of pathologists at exhumations is not acceptable because they are not forensic experts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is no problem, Mr. Milosevic, but as you know quite well, if you're asking a witness about his statement or his report, the witness should have it in front of him. There may be things which you misquote, though maybe not in this case. Now, have you got a copy of that, Doctor? Right. Paragraph 10. What about the -- the question is: Do pathologists have any role at all in exhumations or can they play any part in that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can explain once again the procedure applied and how we in Croatia carried out the process of exhumation and identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Strinovic, let me first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let him finish. Let him answer. Let him answer in his own way and then you can ask some more questions. Yes. Go on, Dr. Strinovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the work attached to exhumation and identification as a rule whenever possible was done by specialists in forensic medicine because they were qualified and trained to do that. Their work consists of establishing causes of death, death caused by violence, identification in cases of natural disasters and so on. So wherever possible, specialists in forensic medicine were used. However, as there was a lot to do and there were so many cases to address, when there were experienced pathologists who had earlier on in their careers engaged in forensic cases, we have forensic medical experts, but in some regions, as in Zadar, an experienced old pathologist who specialises in pathology also is an expert for forensic medicine, so he's also engaged by the courts as an expert. So in such cases, pathologists were also used who assisted specialists in forensic medicine. So when those were lacking and there was a lot to do, we had experienced pathologists, they lent a helping hand and assisted the pathologists. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll continue this after the adjournment. Dr. Strinovic, we're going to adjourn now for 20 minutes. There is one matter I want to deal with, an administrative matter, and it is this, to let the Court know that we will not be sitting in the week after Easter. You can pass that on, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, to the others in your team. We are producing a calendar. You should have it next week, but meanwhile, you should know that in advance. Yes. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Strinovic, my question was very precise: Regarding a pathologist and a specialist in forensic medicine are two quite different specialties, are they not?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So those two different specialists, an expert of forensic medicine is qualified for exhumations and identifications, is he not?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And a pathologist is not qualified for exhumations and identifications, is he?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, there is no written rule or no law that regulates matters in that way. But I repeat again that there are situations and cases, and that was the situation in Croatia, that we did have experienced people, people who during their long careers, did also engage in forensic medicine, and that is why they were qualified enough to be able to do that work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But tell me, please, in your team of physicians that carried out the work which you supervised in the way we have established, how many of them were not experts in forensic medicine?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just now it's difficult for me to give you a precise figure, but really, very few of them, a minimum number of them were of that profile.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are claiming that pathologists are qualified to carry out exhumations and identifications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has given his explanation. We really can't take the matter any further. If there is some point turning on it, you can ask him, but it seems that we've covered it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me clarify then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that establishing the cause of death and the identity of a person is within the sphere of competence of forensic medicine?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As a principle, that is correct, but I have explained why some pathologists are also capable of providing the answers to such questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 21, you say that, "I, as the coordinator of the team for identification, coordinated the work. However, I neither supervised the work of the identification teams, nor did I examine their reports." Does that confirm that you did not assess the quality of the work of the doctors who engaged in the identification? Is that right? Therefore -- yes, please.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My duty was to coordinate this work, and the work itself was done by qualified experts who did not need supervision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you had no direct participation in the identification, did you?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I participated in the identification from 1991/1992, when that kind of identification started, to the present day. I have been working in constantly, continuously, in the team for identification.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When I say "you," I mean your person involvement in the identification. In how many identifications did you take part or, rather, how many persons did you personally identify?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I can't give you the exact number, but certainly the number would be around 1.000 or something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us clear up another matter having to do with these expert findings. When you testified a moment ago, you repeatedly said that this was such-and-such an event when death had occurred on such-and-such a day. For instance, you say in October 1991, or January 1992, et cetera. How were you able to establish when the victims that were exhumed were killed?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is information obtained through the government office, and they were obtained by processing data, but I did not directly participate in the processing of those data. I received those data from the government office, and they obtained them from a number of sources.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you built in those data obtained from the government office and their sources into your report; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, can we agree that it's not up to forensic medical experts to be able to indicate the date and place where a person was killed? You can report on the place where somebody was exhumed but not where someone was killed. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right, but to have a complete picture, we use the data of the government office linked to the date of disappearance and our data obtained through exhumation and subsequent processing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand, Dr. Strinovic. But, for instance, at the beginning among the photographs you showed, you said this was a Serb who was killed because his son was in the army. Was it your job to establish why someone was killed? How do you know that he wasn't killed because he was a Serb? Within the framework of your expertise, do you include justification for the killing of a Serb by explaining that he was killed because his son was in the army? Is that an expert forensic medical finding that you conveyed here or were you just conveying an assumption of yours?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular case, I just commented on the information obtained from the government office, because this was a unique case of a Serb killed in Vocin at the time. And according to the information obtained at the time, the most probable reason for him being killed was the one I gave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But -- I understand, but you are testifying about things that are not part of your expertise. You're just conveying an assumption reached by another body.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is not directly linked to the cause of death or to my work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's exactly what I was saying, that you said something that has nothing to do with your work. Does the same apply to when you said that somebody died from the consequences of mistreatment in the prison at Knin? How could you reach that conclusion? Can you conclude that someone was dead because of injuries he sustained? How can you say that they were consequences of mistreatment in the prison at Knin?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case, I said that this was information we obtained from the District Court in Zadar, and it was quoted from this report from the court. This was not my own conclusion, nor do I have any evidence. It is just what is written in the report of the District Court in Zadar. So it's not my own information. I could not nor did I check it out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is exactly what I wish to establish. In paragraph 22, you say that the report on causes of death applies to cases processed at the Institute for Forensic Medicine in Zagreb or cases that experts from the institute processed in the field. So the report on the cause of death are not a part of the report that you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which report you're talking about, this report we referred to today or this one linked to Zagreb with the table and the exact figures as to the number of cases processed in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you about both.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In relation to Zagreb, I say that it is right. As for the rest, all the findings were taken, including the findings of the pathologist in Zadar who did the autopsies for Skabrinja, for instance, which was an area that he covered. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. That is quite sufficient. And having said that, is it clear that the findings of the pathologist have not been expertly verified and cannot be seriously considered with respect to causes of death and the sources of injuries? Just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can repeat that in this particular case when we're referring to this pathologist, that they were fresh bodies. That is, shortly after death they were autopsied. The cause of death was quite clear. The protocols were clearly written, with clear descriptions, so it is easy to see what the cause of death was. As I was saying, this particular pathologist was a forensic expert in the court in Zadar for many years, and he was a recognised expert in that field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Dr. Strinovic, as Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff asked you whether you did exhumations of killed Serbs, and then she also said she wouldn't go into that because it was not the case of the other side that they're interested in, but you, nevertheless, answered yes, that you did. So tell me, please, did you conduct autopsies of the officers and soldiers of the JNA that were killed?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say yes, and this was in 1991. I think it was sometime in October 1991 when some soldiers in the barracks in Bjelovar were killed, some 20 persons, due to an explosion in the barracks, and both officers and soldiers were killed, of the former JNA. And those cases were processed in Zagreb, and immediately after that, they were handed over to the military authorities in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. But tell me, can you tell us something about the injuries found on their bodies and what kind of weapons were used to provoke those injuries?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not prepared myself to report on these cases that you're asking me about, but to the best of my recollection when we're talking about the Bjelovar barracks, there was a large explosion which caused the death of a large number of people. These were injuries caused by explosive devices. That's all I can say at the moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, then. As a forensic doctor, did you do autopsies of killed Serbs, and how many, where, and when?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just list some cases in which we did process killed Serbs. This was in 1991. Snjegovic, 13 persons, Vukovar Novo Grobija [phoen] where in large grave there are more than 900 persons. Among them were about 70 Serbs that were also processed. Then there is the Paulin Dvor or Zvanusa where 18 bodies were found. Pakracka Poljana, 19 bodies found. The Medacki Dzep, or pocket, 11 bodies that were processed. Karlovac, I think at the bridge, 13 persons who were killed and processed in Zagreb. And after 1995, at the Knin cemetery 300 persons were exhumed, 300 of Serb ethnicity; in Gracac, 154; in Korenica, 27. Those persons were exhumed, processed. And the last group I referred to, consisting of 481 persons, Knin, Gracac, and Korenica, a they were processed. The process of identification is ongoing. 112 persons have been identified from Knin, but the process continues. Relatives are being invited to come from Croatia and Serbia to identify their family members. And the Gracac gravesite has been processed completely. We are now collecting additional information and albums are being prepared which are being sent to where relatives of the missing persons are residing. So we're preparing the identification. The same applies to Korenica. So classical identification is applied as in all other cases, but also DNA identification is done when the relatives are not sure or when the information is unclear, then we use DNA analysis also. So this process of identification of Serbs in Croatia is continuing. It is slow, as applies to identification in general. We have more than 500 bodies at Mirogoj, the cemetery at Zagreb, persons killed ever since 1991. They have not yet been identified. We are trying to establish their identity, but it is a slow process. And the same applies to these cases that I'm referring to now, that is, Croatian citizens of Serb ethnicity whose bodies have been exhumed at these cemeteries that I have listed and for whom the process of identification is ongoing, and we hope we will be able to deal with the problem successfully soon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Talking about the autopsies of killed Serbs, can you say anything very briefly about the injuries found on their bodies and the objects with which those injuries were inflicted?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could give you precise data after a detailed processing or written traces of the same, but what I can say is that they were all types of injuries, mostly gunshot wounds and wounds caused by explosives. As to the other instruments that were used, it's difficult for me to talk about them without any prepared material, written documents. So I can't be more precise on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What other forms of injuries and instruments used?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So after gunshot wounds and explosion wounds, which are the most numerous, there were injuries of the type, for example, of stabs, stabbing wounds, cuts by knives, blunt objects, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So those were the injuries that did not result as the effects of modern weaponry; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would be it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that it, Dr. Strinovic?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't really comment. They are the causes of death that I describe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And did you carry out the autopsy of soldier Marko Utrzan who had been captured as a JNA member, was in a camp in Zagreb and in mid 1991 he was killed by a killer whose identity is known and the bodily remains were handed over to the family members afterwards?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
